Low-spin ground state of the giant single-molecule magnets {Mn70} and {Mn84}

Roman Rausch Affiliation: Technische Universität Braunschweig, Institut für Mathematische Physik, Mendelssohnstraße 3, 38106 Braunschweig, Germany    Christoph Karrasch Affiliation: Technische Universität Braunschweig, Institut für Mathematische Physik, Mendelssohnstraße 3, 38106 Braunschweig, Germany
Abstract

The single-molecule magnets {Mn70} and {Mn84} are characterized by a 14-site unit cell with S=2S=2 spin sites arranged in a circular geometry. Experimentally, these systems exhibit a magnetic ground state with a notably low total spin Stot=5−7S_{\text{tot}}=5-7. Up to now, this low-spin ground state has been up difficult to describe theoretically due to the complexity of the quantum Heisenberg model for such a large system. In this work, we fill this gap and demonstrate that the ground state of {Mn70} and {Mn84} is in fact governed by a small, finite StotS_{\text{tot}} in quantitative agreement with the experiment. We employ accurate, large-scale SU(2)-symmetric density-matrix renormalization group calculations for a quantum Heisenberg model with previously published exchange parameters obtained by density-functional theory. We do not find a low-spin state for the same parameters and S=1S=1 and thus propose that frustrated systems with S≥2S\geq 2 are inherently prone to weak ferromagnetic interactions. This could account for the prevalence of similar low-spin Mn-based single-molecule magnets. Finally, we compute the full magnetization curve and find wide plateaus at 10/14, 11/14, 12/14 and 13/14 of the saturation, which can be traced back to nearly-independent 3-site clusters with broken inter-cluster bonds.

I Introduction

Recent decades saw significant advances in creating large magnetic aggregates [1], which have evolved beyond zero-dimensional molecules and can now often be considered as finite but large condensed-matter systems. A particular highlight is the family of Mn wheel molecules, which have a unit cell of Lcell=14L_{\text{cell}}=14 magnetic centres arranged on a ring (see Fig. 1). The spin sites are Mn3+ ions with S=2S=2. The successfully synthesized variants are {Mn70} [2] and {Mn84} [3, 1] with Ncells=5,6N_{\text{cells}}=5,6 unit cells and L=Lcell⋅NcellsL=L_{\text{cell}}\cdot N_{\text{cells}} total sites. The variants {Mn56} and {Mn98} (Ncells=4,7N_{\text{cells}}=4,7) might also be fabricable [2]. The {Mn84} wheel has set the record as the largest single-molecule magnet (SMM) [1]. Despite the SMM classification, it actually features a relatively small ground-state spin of Stot=6S_{\text{tot}}=6, i.e., Stot/L≈0.07S_{\text{tot}}/L\approx 0.07, Stot/Smax≈0.04S_{\text{tot}}/S_{\text{max}}\approx 0.04 with Smax=S​L=2​LS_{\text{max}}=SL=2L. Similarly, Stot=5−8S_{\text{tot}}=5-8 (Stot/L≈0.07​–​0.11S_{\text{tot}}/L\approx 0.07\text{--}0.11, Stot/Smax≈0.04​–​0.06S_{\text{tot}}/S_{\text{max}}\approx 0.04\text{--}0.06) is found for {Mn70} [2] depending on the experimental extraction procedure and the precise chemical environment. In fact, such a low-spin state is quite typical among Mn-based SMMs. Reported compounds are listed in Tab. 1.

In the absence of anisotropies, localized spins are described by the isotropic Heisenberg model

H=∑i​jJi​j​𝐒i⋅𝐒j−g​μB​B​∑iSiz,H=\sum_{ij}J_{ij}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}-g\mu_{B}B\sum_{i}S^{z}_{i}, (1)

where 𝐒i=(Six,Siy,Siz)\mathbf{S}_{i}=(S^{x}_{i},S^{y}_{i},S^{z}_{i}) is the vector of spin operators at site ii, gg is the gyromagnetic ratio, μB\mu_{B} is the Bohr magneton, and BB is the external field. For a system of LL spins, the interactions are defined by the L×LL\times L matrix Ji​jJ_{ij}, which is best conveyed graphically (see Fig. 1). For B=0B=0, the system has SU(2) invariance and the total spin

∑i​j⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩=⟨𝐒tot2⟩=Stot​(Stot+1)\sum_{ij}\left\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\right\rangle=\left<\mathbf{S}_{\text{tot}}^{2}\right>=S_{\text{tot}}\left(S_{\text{tot}}+1\right) (2)

is a conserved quantity. The total magnetization is given by

Mtot=∑i⟨Siz⟩M_{\text{tot}}=\sum_{i}\langle S^{z}_{i}\rangle (3)

and is a conserved quantity for B≥0B\geq 0.

The theoretical description of large molecules where the number of sites approaches L∼100L\sim 100 poses a challenge to theory. Twenty years ago, the benchmark of theory-experiment comparison was set by Mn12Ac (four sites with S=3/2S=3/2 and eight sites with S=2S=2) whose Hilbert space size is ∼8.6⋅106\sim 8.6\cdot 10^{6} in the subspace Mtot=0M_{\text{tot}}=0 [10, 11, 12]. This problem is amenable to Lanczos diagonalization, so that an extensive comparison with the experiment could be carried out, and the family of these systems was even termed the “drosophila of single-molecule magnetism” [13]. Lanczos diagonalization runs into problems in the case of {Mn84} whose Hilbert space size is ∼1.6⋅1057\sim 1.6\cdot 10^{57} for Mtot=0M_{\text{tot}}=0, and no theoretical progress could be made.

Renewed interest in the {Mn84} wheel from theory came sixteen years after its original discovery [14, 15]. In a pioneering work, density-functional theory (DFT) was used to compute the three dominant exchange integrals J1−3J_{1-3} and the system was subsequently studied in a simplified fashion [14]: The ground state of the {Mn7} subunit was discussed and the full system was treated by coupling coarse-grained subunits. The polarized ground state could not be explained because all the three exchange integrals turned out to be antiferromagnetic, but it was speculated that such a state should arise for longer-ranged ferromagnetic interactions. This approach was refined in a pivotal follow-up work [15], where the first seven exchange integrals J1−7J_{1-7} were computed, and J5J_{5} turned out to be ferromagnetic (see Fig. 1). The specific heat and the magnetization curve were computed in terms of the classical Ising and Potts models by using a geometry-adapted tensor-network representation of the partition function. Up to this point, an accurate treatment of the full quantum Heisenberg model and a clear verification of the low-spin ground state of {Mn84} is still missing.

On a different front, theoretical methods have been pushed in the last years to solve the full problem of large clusters of highly interconnected isotropic quantum spins. E.g., by using large-scale density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations, the long-standing problem of understanding the ground state on the pyrochlore lattice was solved for finite clusters with L=64−128L=64-128 spins (S=1/2,1S=1/2,1) [16, 17]. The caveat is that the restriction to a finite system is still an uncontrolled approximation for lattices (especially in higher dimensions), but no such problem exists for molecules, where a conclusive solution was obtained for up to L=60L=60 spins (S=1/2S=1/2) [18, 19]. A novel competing approach comes from a method based on neural networks [20].

In this paper, we employ large-scale DMRG numerics to significantly extend the previous classical-spin results for {Mn84} with S=2S=2. We show that by exploiting the full SU(2) symmetry of the problem, the full quantum-mechanical Heisenberg model remains tracatable and energy gaps of ∼10−4​J1\sim 10^{-4}J_{1} can be resolved through effective bond dimensions of the order of χeff∼50000\chi_{\text{eff}}\sim 50000. We use the published set of exchange integrals [15], but neglect the small long-range values J6J_{6} and J7J_{7} which complicate the numerics. We demonstrate that the remaining five exchange integrals [15] quantitatively reproduce the low-spin ground state Stot/Ncells≈1S_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}\approx 1 without any additional fitting, thereby closing the gap between theory and experiment.

II Technical details

The DMRG algorithm approximates the ground-state wavefunction as a matrix-product state, capturing entanglement and correlations through iterative optimization and state truncation. The key control parameter is the bond dimension χ\chi that corresponds to the number of variational parameters in the ansatz state. As a rigorous measure of accuracy, we employ the variance per site given by

var/L=|⟨H2J12⟩−⟨HJ1⟩2|/L.\text{var}/L=\bigg|\left<\frac{H^{2}}{J_{1}^{2}}\right>-\left<\frac{H}{J_{1}}\right>^{2}\bigg|/L. (4)

We extrapolate the energy per site by a linear ansatz E/L=(E/L)exact+α⋅var/LE/L=(E/L)_{\text{exact}}+\alpha\cdot\text{var}/L [21]. We use the two-site DMRG algorithm to grow the bond dimension for the first iterations before switching to the cheaper one-site algorithm with perturbations [22]. The system naturally features periodic boundary conditions, which we implement via long-range terms on the level of the matrix-product operator representation of the Hamiltonian, and the bandwidth of the interaction graph Ji​jJ_{ij} is minimized using the reverse Cuthill-McKee algorithm [23, 18].

The SU(2) symmetry of the model (1) with B=0B=0 allows us to increase efficiency by working in the reduced spin basis. A SU(2)-invariant bond dimension χSU(2)\chi_{\text{SU(2)}} corresponds to a much larger effective χeff\chi_{\text{eff}}. For the S=2S=2 system investigated here, we find χeff∼7​χSU(2)\chi_{\text{eff}}\sim 7\chi_{\text{SU(2)}}, i.e., almost an order-of-magnitude gain. Moreover, the exploitation of SU(2) symmetry allows us to directly target states with a given quantum number StotS_{\text{tot}} and compute the energy curve E⁡(Stot)E(S_{\text{tot}}).

As a guiding principle, we will also study a system with an infinite number of unit cells Ncells→∞N_{\text{cells}}\to\infty. To this end, we employ the variational uniform matrix-product state (VUMPS) formalism [24] with a numerical unit cell equal to the Mn14 subunit. As a state error analogous to Eq. (4), we use the two-site variance, see Ref. [24] for details. Within the VUMPS algorithm, we can exploit the SU(2) symmetry but can only access the sector Stot=0S_{\text{tot}}=0 which does not necessarily correspond to the ground in frustrated systems with mixed antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic interactions where the Lieb-Mattis theorem [25] does not hold. One can also exploit only the U(1) symmetry, but this approach restricts polarizations within the unit cell to integer values. If no symmetry is exploited, the algorithm tends to converge to the lowly entangled sector with Mtot=StotM_{\text{tot}}=S_{\text{tot}}, and we can directly compute the total spin per site [21], which might take irrational values. In a nutshell, exploiting different symmetries allows us to perform a cross-diagnostic analysis of the systems.

III Infinite number of unit cells

As a guiding principle for {Mn84}, we first look at an infinite number of unit cells. Figure 2 shows the energies as a function of the state error which decreases with increasing bond dimension, see Ref. [24]. The VUMPS calculation that does not exploit any symmetries yields the lowest energy and a polarization of Mtot/Ncells≈0.96M_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}\approx 0.96. This energy is very close to the one obtained from a U(1) symmetric calculation in the sector Mtot/Ncells=1M_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}=1. The spin singlet Stot=0S_{\text{tot}}=0 accessed by exploiting SU(2) symmetry is also close in energy, but remains slightly above. Higher integer polarizations Mtot/Ncells>1M_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}>1 within the 14-site unit cell clearly correspond to excited states. Note that a U(1)-symmetric calculation with Mtot=0M_{\text{tot}}=0 yields no new information: For a ground state with Stot=0S_{\text{tot}}=0, the results coincide with those of a SU(2)-symmetric calculation, and for one with Stot>0S_{\text{tot}}>0, a degenerate state with Mtot>0M_{\text{tot}}>0 will have lower entanglement.

We conclude that the ground state of the system features an irrational polarization close to, but not exactly equal to Mtot/Ncells=1M_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}=1, with a small energy barrier towards the singlet. For finite systems up to L=84L=84 where the total spin can only change in integer steps, we expect a ground state with Stot/Ncells=1S_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}=1, i.e., the integer spin closest to Stot/Ncells≈0.96S_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}\approx 0.96.

IV Finite rings

We now turn to finite rings of Ncells=2−6N_{\text{cells}}=2-6 unit cells with periodic boundary conditions; recall that Ncells=6N_{\text{cells}}=6 corresponds to {Mn84}. We use the SU(2)-symmetric DMRG algorithm to compute the lowest energy in each spin sector in the range Stot=0−8S_{\text{tot}}=0-8. This is shown in Fig. 3, which is the central result of our work.

For Ncells=2,3,4N_{\text{cells}}=2,3,4, a bond dimension of χSU(2)≤4000\chi_{\text{SU(2)}}\leq 4000 is sufficient to obtain converged data. The variance per site is of the order of 10−4​meV210^{-4}\text{meV}^{2} for χSU(2)=4000\chi_{\text{SU(2)}}=4000. For Ncells=5,6N_{\text{cells}}=5,6, which correspond to the physical cases of {Mn70} and {Mn84}, the gaps become smaller and we have to go up to χSU(2)=8000\chi_{\text{SU(2)}}=8000 to obtain the same accuracy. In all cases, the true ground state features Stot/Ncells=1S_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}=1. However, Stot=5S_{\text{tot}}=5 and Stot=6S_{\text{tot}}=6 are extremely close in energy for {Mn84}, and Stot=6S_{\text{tot}}=6 only wins by a very small margin for χSU(2)=8000\chi_{\text{SU(2)}}=8000. A conservative estimate is that Stot=5,6S_{\text{tot}}=5,6 are near-degenerate for {Mn84} with an energy per site of E/(L​J1)=−1.8148±0.0002E/(LJ_{1})=-1.8148\pm 0.0002.

Overall, our large-scale DMRG calculations paired with exchange integrals from DFT decisively confirm the experimentally-measured total-spin state of {Mn84}. We emphasize that in order to tackle this problem, it was imperative to employ a state-of-the art, SU(2) symmetric algorithm and bond dimensions of up to χSU(2)=8000\chi_{\text{SU(2)}}=8000 which corresponds to a much larger χeff∼50000\chi_{\text{eff}}\sim 50000. There may still be some influence from factors we have neglected, such as the inclusion of longer-ranged couplings or distortions in the interatomic distances. We hypothesize that these additional influences are small enough to preserve the general shape of the Stot/Ncells≈1S_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}\approx 1 minimum.

V Dependence on the spin quantum number

We briefly test whether a hypothetical S=1S=1 system on the same geometry and with the same exchange parameters would also feature a ground state with a finite but small value of the total spin. Figure 4 shows the lowest energy in different sectors of StotS_{\text{tot}} for L=56,70,84L=56,70,84. A bond dimension of χSU(2)=2000\chi_{\text{SU(2)}}=2000 is sufficient to obtain a variance per site of the order of 10−5​meV210^{-5}\text{meV}^{2}. We find that the overall minimum (i.e., the true ground state) is always at Stot=0S_{\text{tot}}=0. The infinite-system calculation similarly shows Mtot≈0M_{\text{tot}}\approx 0 (inset to Fig. 4).

We conclude that for an S=1S=1 system, the singlet ground state is robust against weak ferromagnetic perturbations, whereas it becomes susceptible to them in the case of S=2S=2 and leads to a polarized ground state. Intuitively, it is clear that due to a large number of internal states, a high spin can “afford” a coexistence of a partial polarization and quantum fluctuations to minimize the energy, and in this sense becomes more classical. The non-trivial result is that this transition happens between S=1S=1 and S=2S=2. This observation may explain the multitude of low-spin Mn-based SMMs listed in Tab. 1, where the Mn sites have a local spin value that varies in the range S=2±0.5S=2\pm 0.5 depending on the oxidation state (Mn2+ to Mn4+).

VI Magnetization curve

In this section we compute the magnetization curve for finite magnetic fields. We can determine the ground state of HH by first computing the lowest-energy eigenstates |Stot⟩|S_{\text{tot}}\rangle at B=0B=0 for all values of Stot=0​…​2​LS_{\text{tot}}=0...2L using a SU(2)-symmetric algorithm. These are also eigenstates at finite BB, and the overall ground state can be obtained by minimizing

⟨Stot|H⁡(B=0)|Stot⟩−g​μB​B​Stot\langle S_{\text{tot}}|H(B=0)|S_{\text{tot}}\rangle-g\mu_{B}BS_{\text{tot}} (5)

w.r.t. StotS_{\text{tot}}; note that the second term in Eq. (1) becomes minimal for Mtot=StotM_{\text{tot}}=S_{\text{tot}}. Since this is a large volume of computations, we limit ourselves to χSU(2)=1000\chi_{\text{SU(2)}}=1000. However, the full spectrum is on an energy scale of >4500​meV>4500\text{meV}, so that sub-meV energy inaccuracies carry no weight in this case. Moreover, the reduced Hilbert space at high spins makes the calculations easier and we find that all the energies with Stot≳114S_{\text{tot}}\gtrsim 114 for L=84L=84 are in fact numerically exact for this bond dimension.

Figure 5 shows the magnetization MtotM_{\text{tot}} as a function of the magnetic field for L=56,70,84L=56,70,84. Starting from the zero-field limit Mtot​(B→0)=NcellsM_{\text{tot}}(B\to 0)=N_{\text{cells}}, we observe a linear increase (with small finite-size steps) until g​μB​B∼16​meVg\mu_{B}B\sim 16\text{meV}, i.e., until the field becomes larger than the dominant exchange J1=13​meVJ_{1}=13\text{meV}. This is followed by a wide plateau at 10/14 of the saturation, and again by three more narrow plateaus at 11/14, 12/14, and 13/14. We note that due to the large value of J1J_{1} (which corresponds to T≈151​K/kBT\approx 151\text{K}/k_{B}), even the first plateau will be quite difficult to observe, requiring at least B∼160​TB\sim 160\text{T}.

In order to better understand the origin of the plateaus, we compute the site-resolved magnetizations ⟨Siz⟩\left<S^{z}_{i}\right> and find that the tetrahedra at these plateaus are almost completely polarized with Mtetra≈8M_{\text{tetra}}\approx 8. This is understandable because the coupling J3=1.1​meVJ_{3}=1.1\text{meV} is weak. Since the line pieces are coupled via the tetrahedra (see Fig. 1), they disconnect and the physics should be governed by an ensemble of independent 3-site clusters described by the Hamiltonian

Heff=J⁡(𝐒1⋅𝐒2+𝐒2⋅𝐒3)−g​μB​B​∑i=13Siz.H_{\text{eff}}=J\left(\mathbf{S}_{1}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{2}+\mathbf{S}_{2}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{3}\right)-g\mu_{B}B\sum_{i=1}^{3}S^{z}_{i}. (6)

To support this hypothesis, we compute the magnetization curve of HeffH_{\text{eff}} for S=2S=2 [see Fig. 6 b)] and find a 2/6 plateau of width g​μB​Δ​B=3​Jg\mu_{B}\Delta B=3J as well as three plateaus at 3/6, 4/6, 5/6 of width g​μB​Δ​B=Jg\mu_{B}\Delta B=J. The central spin aligns itself antiparallel to the others to maximize the exchange energy and is flipped in a stepwise fashion. This quantitatively explains the number and widths of the plateaus for the full case in Fig. 5 if one sets J=J1=13​meVJ=J_{1}=13\text{meV} and rescales the fraction of the saturation by including the tetrahedra M/Msat=(n+8)/(6+8)M/M_{\text{sat}}=(n+8)/(6+8), n=2,3,4,5n=2,3,4,5.

Magnetization plateaus are typically related to localized magnons, where spinflips localize due to a canceling of hopping terms on a frustrated geometry [26, 27, 28, 29]. In our case, the reason for localization is the inhomogeneous form of the interactions; the external field divides the system into independent islands by breaking the weak bonds that connect them. A similar effect was observed in Atacamite [30].

VII Conclusion

We have studied the quantum Heisenberg model on the geometry of the Mn giant wheels using a set of DFT-computed exchange parameters [15] combined with large-scale SU(2)-symmetric DMRG calculations where the effective bond dimension reaches values of χeff∼50000\chi_{\text{eff}}\sim 50000. The presence of a unit cell allows us to scale the system size from finite rings with Ncells=2−6N_{\text{cells}}=2-6 and also to compare with the infinite chain as a guiding case. The ground state clearly features a total spin Stot/Ncells≈1S_{\text{tot}}/N_{\text{cells}}\approx 1, which quantitatively reproduces the experimental values (Stot=6S_{\text{tot}}=6 for {Mn84}, Ncells=6N_{\text{cells}}=6) without any additional free parameters. This shows that theory has caught up with experimental progress in manufacturing high-nucleation SMMs and is able to successfully describe large finite magnetic systems with L∼100L\sim 100 spin sites.

By reducing the spin quantum number to S=1S=1, we find that the ground state robustly remains at Stot=0S_{\text{tot}}=0. We hence argue that systems with S≳2S\gtrsim 2 become susceptible to the presence of small ferromagnetic exchange interactions and react by a partial ground-state polarization. This explains the multitude of low-spin SMMs that are based on Mn ions and marks a crossover point from quantum to classical spins; the low-spin state emerges from a delicate interplay of three key factors, all of which are essential: i) the presence of a small ferromagnetic coupling, ii) frustration, and iii) a spin S>1S>1.

Finally, we find magnetization plateaus at 10/14, 11/14, 12/14 and 13/14 of the saturation; they are a consequence of the inhomogeous interactions in the system and can be explained by independent 3-site clusters whose weak inter-cluster couplings are broken by the external field.
